nameStory: The Northeastern Lucine gets its name from its location along the northeastern Atlantic coast and its membership in the lucine clam family. The word 'lucine' comes from the Latin 'lucina,' meaning 'she who brings to light,' possibly referring to the pale, almost luminous appearance of these shells when cleaned. The species name 'filosa' means 'thread-like,' describing the fine growth lines that trace across the shell surface.
description: The Northeastern Lucine is a small, round clam that lives buried in muddy sea bottoms along New England's coast. This delicate bivalve has a nearly circular shell that typically grows to about 1-2 inches across, with a glossy white or cream-colored surface. Unlike the common clams you might find at a clambake, lucines have thin, lightweight shells with a distinctly rounded shape. They're part of a specialized group of clams that have developed unique relationships with bacteria in their gills to help them survive in low-oxygen environments.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Nearly perfectly round shell that feels surprisingly light and delicate in your hand, like holding a small porcelain dish

idTips.label: Shell Color
idTips.description: Clean white to cream colored exterior with a glossy, almost pearlescent finish that catches light beautifully

idTips.label: Growth Lines
idTips.description: Very fine, thread-like concentric rings across the shell surface that you can feel with your fingertip like tiny ridges

idTips.label: Shell Thickness
idTips.description: Noticeably thin and lightweight compared to other clams of similar size - feels almost fragile when handled

idTips.label: Hinge Area
idTips.description: Small, triangular teeth near the shell's hinge that interlock precisely when the shell closes

habitat: Found in soft, muddy bottoms of shallow coastal waters and deeper offshore areas from the Gulf of Maine southward. They prefer areas with low oxygen levels where their bacterial partners can thrive, often in deeper waters beyond typical beachcombing zones. Most specimens wash ashore after storms or are brought up in fishing nets rather than being found alive by casual collectors.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash up on beaches after spring storms, appearing bright white and intact. This is often the best time to find pristine specimens as winter waves uncover buried shells.
seasonality.summer: Living clams are active in offshore waters, but beach finds become less common. Any shells found are likely weathered from extended beach exposure.
seasonality.fall: Another good season for beach discoveries as autumn storms churn up the sea bottom and deposit shells on shore. Look for them mixed in with other storm debris.
seasonality.winter: Clams retreat deeper into sediment during cold months. Beach searching is most productive after major winter storms that disturb deep offshore sediments.

funFact: Northeastern Lucines are like tiny underwater farmers - they actually cultivate bacteria in their gills that convert toxic hydrogen sulfide from the muddy sea bottom into food, allowing them to thrive in environments that would poison most other clams.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small quahog clams, but lucines are much more perfectly round and feel noticeably lighter and more fragile. Remember: 'Lucines are light and round like little moons' - if it feels heavy for its size, it's probably a young quahog.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Northeastern,' this species is actually at the northern edge of its range in New England waters and becomes more common further south. The extremely low observation count in New England reflects both their preference for deeper waters and their status as a somewhat tropical species reaching its limit here.
compareHints: As the only Lucinoma species regularly found in New England waters, compare it with other lucine family members like the buttercup lucine, which is smaller and more yellow-tinted. The Northeastern Lucine is distinguished by its larger size, pure white color, and more pronounced thread-like growth lines. Other local clams in different families will feel much heavier and have more oval or elongated shapes rather than the lucine's distinctive round profile.
